Separation of Mixtures and Purification.intro: A mixture contains two or more substances physically combined; its components retain their properties and can be separated by physical methods. A pure substance has a fixed composition and characteristic properties.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Selecting a method from physical properties; Distillation and crystallization in practice; and Chromatography and purity.

Choose a technique from differences in particle size, solubility, boiling point, volatility, magnetism or affinity for a surface. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; evaporation/crystallization recovers dissolved solids; simple distillation recovers a solvent or separates liquids with widely different boiling points; fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with closer boiling points. A separating funnel handles immiscible liquids. Sublimation separates a sublimable solid. Chromatography separates substances by different attractions to stationary and mobile phases; Rf = distance travelled by spot/distance travelled by solvent front.

To separate sand and salt: add water to dissolve salt, filter off sand, wash and dry the residue, then evaporate the filtrate carefully to crystallize salt. To obtain pure water as well, distil the filtrate and collect the distillate.

blocks.x: 3. Selecting a method from physical properties

Begin by identifying the phases and the property that differs. Filtration works only when a solid is insoluble; dissolved particles pass through filter paper. Crystallization depends on a change in solubility with temperature. Distillation separates through different boiling behaviour, while chromatography depends on relative attraction to two phases. A magnet works only if one component is magnetic.

In simple distillation, heat the mixture so the more volatile component vaporizes, then cool the vapour in a condenser. Fractional distillation uses a column that repeatedly vaporizes and condenses components; the lower-boiling liquid becomes richer in the rising vapour. To crystallize, concentrate a hot saturated solution, cool it slowly, collect crystals, rinse with a little cold solvent and dry them.

A spot separates because components partition differently between stationary and mobile phases. Keep the sample small, use a pencil baseline because ink can dissolve, and keep the solvent below the baseline. A pure substance usually gives one spot under a particular solvent system; multiple spots suggest a mixture. Rf values are comparable only under the same experimental conditions.

Chemical Combination.intro: Chemical combination describes how elements and compounds react in fixed proportions to form new substances. Equations summarize reactants, products and conservation of atoms.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Balancing equations and mole ratios; Limiting reactant and yield; and Empirical and molecular formula.

The law of conservation of mass says total mass is conserved in a closed chemical reaction. Definite proportions: a pure compound contains its elements in a fixed mass ratio. Multiple proportions: when two elements form several compounds, masses combining with a fixed mass of one element are in simple whole-number ratios. Relative atomic mass Ar and relative formula mass Mr have no units; amount n=m/M and particle count N=nNA, where NA≈6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. Balance equations by changing coefficients, never subscripts.
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O conserves four H atoms and two O atoms on both sides. For 18 g water, n=m/Mr=18/18=1 mol.

A balanced equation expresses a particle ratio, not equal masses. Coefficients give mole ratios: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O means 2 mol hydrogen reacts with 1 mol oxygen to form 2 mol water. Convert a known mass to moles first, use the coefficient ratio, then convert the required amount back to mass or volume.

The limiting reactant is used up first and sets the maximum product. Calculate the available moles of each reactant divided by its coefficient; the smallest value identifies the limiting substance. Theoretical yield is the maximum predicted amount; percentage yield compares actual with theoretical yield and may be reduced by incomplete reaction, side reactions or product loss.

An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number atom ratio. Convert each element's mass or percentage to moles, divide all by the smallest amount, and scale ratios to whole numbers. Molecular formula is an integer multiple of the empirical formula, found from molecular mass divided by empirical formula mass.

Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas Laws.intro: The kinetic particle model explains states of matter and gas behaviour using moving particles. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of particles.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Heating and phase changes; Deriving gas-law patterns; and Diffusion and relative molecular mass.

Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions; liquid particles remain close but move past one another; gas particles are far apart and move randomly. Gas pressure comes from particle collisions with container walls. Boyle’s law pV=constant at fixed T; Charles’ law V/T=constant at fixed p; pressure law p/T=constant at fixed V. Combined law p₁V₁/T₁=p₂V₂/T₂; ideal gas equation pV=nRT. Use kelvin. Diffusion is faster at higher temperature and lower relative molecular mass; Graham’s law gives rate ∝1/√Mr.
A 2.0 L gas at 300 K is heated to 450 K at constant pressure: V₂=2.0×450/300=3.0 L.

When a solid is warmed, particle vibration increases; at melting, energy changes arrangement rather than temperature. In a liquid, particles can move past one another; in a gas, widely separated particles move rapidly and randomly. Boiling and evaporation differ: boiling occurs throughout when vapour pressure matches external pressure, while evaporation occurs at the surface below boiling point.

At constant temperature, decreasing gas volume increases collision frequency with the walls and pressure (Boyle). At constant pressure, temperature rises in kelvin and particles move faster, so volume must rise (Charles). At fixed volume, faster collisions raise pressure (pressure law). These arguments assume a fixed amount of gas and approximately ideal behaviour.

Gas particles diffuse down a concentration gradient by random motion. At equal temperature and pressure, lighter molecules have higher average speeds and diffuse faster. Graham's law gives r₁/r₂=√(Mr₂/Mr₁). Real gases depart from the ideal model at high pressure or low temperature because particle volume and attractions become important.

Atomic Structure and Bonding.intro: Atoms contain a tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons. Chemical bonding results from electrostatic attractions involving valence electrons and helps atoms reach more stable arrangements.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Electron arrangement and periodic patterns; Ionic and covalent structure; and Metallic bonding and polarity.

Protons have charge +1 and relative mass 1; neutrons charge 0 and mass 1; electrons charge −1 and tiny relative mass. Atomic number Z=protons; mass number A=protons+neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron numbers. Ionic bonding transfers electrons and creates oppositely charged ions; covalent bonding shares electron pairs; metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons. Bonding and structure explain properties: ionic solids conduct when molten/aqueous, metals conduct as solids, simple molecular substances often have low melting points.
For ²³₁₁Na, protons=11, electrons=11 in a neutral atom, neutrons=23−11=12. Sodium chloride forms Na⁺ and Cl⁻ by electron transfer.

blocks.x: Electrons occupy shells or energy levels; for the first 20 elements, the simple shell pattern fills 2, then 8, then 8 before the next shell. The outer-shell electron number helps predict valency and common ion charge. Elements in the same group have similar outer electron arrangements and therefore related chemical properties. Across a period, nuclear charge generally rises while electrons enter the same main shell.

Ionic compounds form a giant lattice of alternating ions; strong electrostatic forces act in all directions, giving high melting points. They conduct only when ions can move (molten or dissolved). Simple covalent molecules have strong bonds inside molecules but weaker forces between molecules, so they often melt at lower temperatures and do not conduct. Giant covalent structures such as diamond are exceptions.

Metallic solids contain positive ion cores in a sea of delocalized electrons, explaining conductivity and malleability. Covalent bonds share electron pairs; unequal sharing creates polar bonds when electronegativity differs. Molecular shape determines whether bond dipoles cancel, affecting solubility and intermolecular attraction.

Air.intro: Air is a mixture of gases, not a compound. Its composition is approximately constant in clean, dry lower-atmosphere air, though water vapour and pollutants vary.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Obtaining gases from air; Combustion and oxides; and Composition and changing atmosphere.

Dry air contains about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, with trace gases. Oxygen supports combustion and respiration; nitrogen is relatively unreactive and used industrially to make ammonia; carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis and contributes to the greenhouse effect. Air can be liquefied and separated by fractional distillation after purification and cooling. Combustion in sufficient oxygen usually gives CO₂ and H₂O for hydrocarbons; limited oxygen may produce CO or soot.
Complete combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. For 1 mol CH₄, 2 mol O₂ are required by the balanced equation.

Air is purified to remove dust, water vapour and carbon dioxide, then cooled and compressed until it liquefies. Fractional distillation separates liquid air because nitrogen and oxygen have different boiling points. Nitrogen, with the lower boiling point, vaporizes first; oxygen-rich liquid remains longer. The separation is physical because air is a mixture, not a compound.

Sufficient oxygen gives complete combustion of many fuels; limited oxygen can produce carbon monoxide and carbon. Carbon monoxide binds strongly to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport. Sulfur in fuel forms sulfur dioxide; high-temperature engines form nitrogen oxides. These gases have health and environmental effects and can be reduced by cleaner fuels and emission controls.

The approximate nitrogen and oxygen percentages refer to clean, dry lower-atmosphere air. Water vapour varies with weather. Carbon dioxide is a small but climatically important component. Plants consume CO₂ in photosynthesis; respiration and combustion return it. Atmospheric composition can be changed locally by pollution and globally by greenhouse-gas emissions.

Water.intro: Water is a polar covalent molecule and an effective solvent for many ionic and polar substances. Its unusual thermal and density properties are important in nature.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Purification and potability; Hardness and softening; and Water as a solvent and reagent.

Pure water is H₂O; hydrogen bonding contributes to its high boiling point, surface tension and heat capacity. Water has maximum density near 4°C and expands on freezing. Hard water contains Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions: temporary hardness is commonly due to hydrogencarbonates and can be removed by boiling; permanent hardness from sulfates/chlorides can be softened chemically or by ion exchange. Potable water is safe for drinking, not necessarily chemically pure. Treatment can include sedimentation, filtration and disinfection.
Temporary hardness can be removed by heating: Ca(HCO₃)₂(aq) → CaCO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l). Insoluble CaCO₃ forms scale.

Water treatment aims to remove suspended solids, dissolved contaminants and pathogens. Sedimentation allows dense particles to settle; filtration removes remaining suspended matter; disinfection such as chlorination kills many microbes. Treatment does not necessarily remove all dissolved salts. Potable water is safe to drink, whereas chemically pure water contains essentially only H₂O.

Temporary hardness results mainly from dissolved calcium or magnesium hydrogencarbonates and can be reduced by boiling as insoluble carbonates form. Permanent hardness is commonly associated with sulfates or chlorides. Washing soda precipitates calcium carbonate; ion-exchange resins replace Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ with Na⁺. Hard water wastes soap by forming scum and can build scale in boilers.
5. Water as a solvent and reagent

Water's polarity allows it to surround ions and dissolve many ionic compounds. It participates in hydration, hydrolysis and acid-base chemistry. Its high specific heat capacity means large energy is needed to change its temperature; ice's lower density makes it float, insulating water beneath.

Solubility.intro: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Reading solubility curves; Concentration and dilution; and Factors affecting dissolution.

Solubility is commonly expressed as grams of solute per 100 g solvent. An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute; a saturated solution is at equilibrium with undissolved solute; a supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than normally stable and crystallizes readily. For most solids, solubility rises with temperature, but not always; gas solubility usually falls as temperature rises and increases with pressure. A solubility curve supports crystallization and mass calculations. Concentration c=n/V in mol dm⁻³, with V in dm³.
If 36 g of solute dissolves in 100 g water at a stated temperature, solubility is 36 g per 100 g water at that temperature.

A solubility curve plots the maximum dissolved solute against temperature for a fixed amount of solvent. A point below the curve represents an unsaturated solution; a point on it is saturated; a point above may represent a supersaturated solution. Cooling a hot saturated solution can crystallize solute; the mass crystallized is the difference between hot and cold solubilities for the same solvent mass.

Molar concentration c=n/V, where volume is in dm³. For dilution with no solute loss, n stays constant, so c₁V₁=c₂V₂. This relation is also used to prepare a dilute solution from a stock. Solubility is a maximum equilibrium amount; concentration is the actual amount per volume and can be below saturation.

Stirring and crushing increase how quickly a solute dissolves by improving contact and surface area, but they do not usually change the equilibrium solubility at a given temperature. For gases, increasing pressure raises solubility; warming usually lowers it. Temperature effects on solid solubility depend on the particular solute.

Environmental Pollution.intro: Pollution occurs when harmful substances or energy enter the environment at levels that damage organisms or ecosystems. Chemistry helps identify pollutants, their sources and ways to reduce them.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Air pollution and atmospheric chemistry; Water pollution and eutrophication; and Monitoring and prevention.

Air pollutants include CO, SO₂, nitrogen oxides, particulates and excess greenhouse gases. SO₂ and NOx can form acid rain; particulates harm respiratory health; excess greenhouse gases enhance warming. Water pollutants include sewage, fertilizers, pesticides, oil and toxic metals. Nitrate/phosphate enrichment can cause eutrophication: algal growth, decomposition and oxygen depletion. Solid waste can be reduced by refusing, reducing, reusing and recycling. Pollution control targets source reduction, treatment and safe disposal.
Combustion of sulfur-containing fuel produces SO₂; oxidation and reaction with water can form acids that lower rainwater pH and damage ecosystems.

Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve or react in atmospheric water to form acidic species, contributing to acid deposition. Acidification damages aquatic life, soils and limestone buildings. Particulate matter penetrates respiratory systems. Carbon dioxide and methane absorb infrared radiation and enhance the greenhouse effect; this differs from ozone depletion, which is mainly associated with certain halogenated compounds.

Sewage introduces organic matter and microbes; decomposition raises biological oxygen demand. Fertilizers add nitrate and phosphate, causing algal blooms. When algae die, decomposers consume dissolved oxygen, creating hypoxic conditions. Toxic metals and persistent pesticides may accumulate through food chains. Treatment should reduce pollutants before discharge rather than rely on dilution.

Scientists measure pH, dissolved oxygen, pollutant concentration, turbidity and biological indicators. Source control includes cleaner fuels, catalytic converters, wastewater treatment, controlled fertilizer application and safe waste handling. The best response depends on the pollutant's persistence, toxicity and pathway through the ecosystem.

Acids, Bases and Salts.intro: Acids and bases are identified by how they behave in water and in reactions. Neutralization produces salt and water when an acid reacts with a base.

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Indicators and pH; Preparing salts; and Titration calculations.

In aqueous solution, acids donate H⁺ (more accurately form H₃O⁺); bases accept H⁺, while alkalis are soluble bases producing OH⁻. Strong/weak refers to degree of ionization, not concentration. pH=−log₁₀[H⁺]; pH below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline at 25°C. Acid + metal → salt + H₂; acid + carbonate → salt + CO₂ + H₂O; acid + base/alkali → salt + water. Salt names depend on acid: hydrochloric → chloride; sulfuric → sulfate; nitric → nitrate. Titration determines reacting volumes/concentration.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. One mole sulfuric acid neutralizes two moles sodium hydroxide.

Oxidation and Reduction.intro: Redox reactions involve electron transfer or changes in oxidation number. Oxidation and reduction always occur together because electrons lost by one species are gained by another.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Oxidation numbers; Half-equations; and Agents and applications.

Oxidation can mean electron loss, oxidation-number increase or addition of oxygen/removal of hydrogen. Reduction means electron gain, oxidation-number decrease or removal of oxygen/addition of hydrogen. OIL RIG is a useful reminder: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons. Oxidizing agents accept electrons and are reduced; reducing agents donate electrons and are oxidized. Oxidation-number rules help identify redox: free elements 0, monatomic ions equal their charge, oxygen usually −2, hydrogen usually +1, and totals match the species charge.
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Zn loses 2e⁻ and is oxidized; Cu²⁺ gains 2e⁻ and is reduced. Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent.

Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping charges assigned by rules. An element in its standard form has oxidation number zero; a monatomic ion has its charge; oxygen is usually −2 and hydrogen usually +1. The sum equals the overall species charge. An increase in oxidation number indicates oxidation; a decrease indicates reduction.

Write separate oxidation and reduction half-equations to show electron transfer. Balance atoms other than H and O first; balance O with water and H with H⁺ in acidic solution, then balance charge with electrons. In alkaline solution, add OH⁻ to neutralize H⁺ and simplify water. Electrons lost must equal electrons gained when half-equations are combined.

An oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidized. Redox occurs in combustion, metal extraction, corrosion, batteries and electrolysis. In a displacement reaction, the more reactive metal is oxidized while ions of the less reactive metal are reduced.

The electrolyte contains mobile ions. Cations migrate to the cathode (negative electrode) and gain electrons; anions migrate to the anode (positive electrode) and lose electrons. Products depend on ions present, concentration and electrode type. In aqueous solutions, hydrogen may form instead of a reactive metal at the cathode; halides may be discharged at the anode when concentrated, otherwise oxygen can form. Energy Changes.intro: Chemical reactions involve energy changes as bonds break and form. Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases energy.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Reaction profiles and activation energy; Bond enthalpy reasoning; and Calorimetry and Hess' law.

An exothermic reaction transfers heat to surroundings and has ΔH<0; an endothermic reaction absorbs heat and has ΔH>0. For bond enthalpies, ΔH≈Σ(bonds broken)−Σ(bonds formed). Reaction profiles show activation energy Ea and enthalpy change. A catalyst lowers activation energy but does not change ΔH or the equilibrium position. Calorimetry estimates heat change using q=mcΔT; molar enthalpy change is ΔH=−q/n for the reacting amount in a simple insulated experiment.
If breaking reactant bonds needs 800 kJ mol⁻¹ and forming product bonds releases 950 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH≈800−950=−150 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic).

A reaction profile plots energy against reaction progress. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to reach the transition state. Exothermic products lie lower in enthalpy than reactants; endothermic products lie higher. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, while the enthalpy difference between starting and final states remains the same.

Breaking bonds absorbs energy because atoms must be separated; making bonds releases energy. Estimate reaction enthalpy by adding bond energies broken and subtracting energies formed. Values are average gas-phase bond enthalpies, so the answer is an estimate. A negative result indicates net release of energy.

In a simple calorimetry experiment, measure temperature change of a known mass and calculate q=mcΔT. Divide by moles reacted for molar enthalpy and reverse sign for reaction versus surroundings. Hess' law says total enthalpy change is independent of route because enthalpy is a state function; combine equations algebraically to find unknown changes.

Rates of Chemical Reaction.intro: Reaction rate measures how quickly reactants are used or products are formed. Collision theory explains rate in terms of successful particle collisions.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Measuring rate; Collision theory and factors; and Experimental fairness.

Particles must collide with sufficient energy (at least activation energy) and suitable orientation. Rate increases with concentration, gas pressure, temperature, surface area of a solid and addition of a suitable catalyst. A catalyst offers a lower-activation-energy pathway and is regenerated. Rate may be measured as amount or concentration change per time, gas volume per time, mass loss per time or colour change. On a concentration-time graph, gradient gives rate; the curve flattens as reactants are consumed.
Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than equal-mass chips with acid because more surface is exposed for collisions each second.

Rate can be determined from change in concentration per time or from a measurable proxy: gas volume, mass loss, precipitate appearance or colour intensity. Plot the measured quantity against time; the gradient gives rate. A steep initial gradient means high initial rate, and a plateau indicates reaction completion or equilibrium depending on the system.

A reaction occurs only when particles collide with enough energy to overcome activation energy and suitable orientation. Higher concentration/pressure increases collision frequency; greater surface area exposes more solid particles; higher temperature increases both collision frequency and the fraction above activation energy. A catalyst lowers the energy barrier without being consumed overall.

To test one factor, hold other conditions constant: same total volume, temperature, reactant masses and apparatus. Use repeats and compare initial rates. Powdered solids react faster than equal-mass lumps because more surface is exposed, not because the powder has more reactant particles in total.

Chemical Equilibrium.intro: A reversible reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium in a closed system when forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. Concentrations remain constant, but reactions continue microscopically.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Dynamic equilibrium and equilibrium constants; Applying Le Chatelier's principle; and Industrial equilibrium.

For aA+bB ⇌ cC+dD, Kc=[C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b), using equilibrium concentrations and omitting pure solids/liquids. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not change Kc or equilibrium composition. Le Chatelier’s principle: a system shifts to oppose an imposed concentration, pressure or temperature change. Increasing pressure favors the side with fewer gas moles; increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction. Only temperature changes Kc.
For N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward NH₃ because 2 gas moles are formed from 4 gas moles.

At equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates. Concentrations are constant but generally not equal. For a given reaction and temperature, Kc has a fixed value. A large Kc indicates products are favoured at equilibrium; a small value indicates reactants are favoured, though actual concentrations also depend on starting quantities.

A concentration increase shifts the reaction to consume some added species. For gases, increased pressure by reducing volume favours the side with fewer gaseous particles; if both sides have equal gas moles, pressure has no shift effect. Heating favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst does not shift equilibrium, it speeds both directions.

The Haber process is exothermic and produces fewer gas moles on the product side, so lower temperature and higher pressure favour ammonia yield. Industry uses moderate temperature for acceptable rate, high but economically practical pressure, an iron catalyst and recycling of unreacted gases.

Non-Metals and Their Compounds.intro: Non-metals are generally poor conductors and tend to gain or share electrons, but their properties vary widely. Their compounds are central to air, water, agriculture and industry.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen; Carbon and sulfur chemistry; and Chlorine and ammonia.

Hydrogen forms water and acids; oxygen supports combustion and forms oxides; nitrogen forms ammonia and nitrates; carbon forms CO₂, CO and an extensive range of covalent compounds; sulfur forms SO₂, SO₃ and sulfuric acid; chlorine forms chlorides and is a disinfectant. Many non-metal oxides are acidic and react with bases to form salts. Ammonia is a basic gas, highly soluble in water, and manufactured by the Haber process: N₂+3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (iron catalyst, elevated pressure and temperature as a compromise).
CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O; limewater turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms.

Hydrogen is a diatomic, flammable gas and can act as a reducing agent. Oxygen supports combustion and is prepared in the laboratory by decomposition of suitable oxygen-rich compounds. Nitrogen is comparatively unreactive due to the strong N≡N bond; industrially it reacts with hydrogen in the Haber process. Their oxides show different acid-base behaviour.

Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide and turns limewater milky; carbon monoxide is a toxic reducing gas from incomplete combustion. Sulfur burns to sulfur dioxide, which can be oxidized to sulfur trioxide and converted to sulfuric acid. These compounds are industrially useful but emissions need control.

Chlorine is a reactive halogen, used to disinfect water and make chlorides; its toxicity requires careful handling. Ammonia is a pungent basic gas, very soluble in water and less dense than air. It reacts with acids to form ammonium salts and is a key fertilizer feedstock.

Metals and Their Compounds.intro: Metals generally conduct heat and electricity, are malleable and form positive ions. Their reactivity determines extraction methods and many displacement reactions.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Reactivity and displacement; Extraction and refining; and Corrosion, protection and alloys.

The reactivity series commonly orders K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au from more to less reactive. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound. Metals above carbon are often extracted by electrolysis; less reactive metals can often be reduced from oxides with carbon or carbon monoxide. Ores are concentrated, converted to suitable compounds and refined. Corrosion of iron needs oxygen and water; painting, oiling, galvanizing and sacrificial protection reduce it. Alloys alter properties by disrupting regular layers of metal atoms.
Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from solution.

A more reactive metal loses electrons more readily. It displaces a less reactive metal from its aqueous salt; no reaction occurs if the added metal is less reactive. Metals above hydrogen often release H₂ from dilute acids. Potassium, sodium and calcium react vigorously with water; metals lower in the series react less or not at all under ordinary conditions.

Very reactive metals are extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds because carbon cannot reduce their stable ions. Metals below carbon may be extracted by heating oxides with carbon or carbon monoxide. Impure ores are concentrated first. Electrorefining can produce high-purity copper by transferring copper from an impure anode to a pure cathode.

Rusting requires oxygen and water and forms hydrated iron(III) oxide. Painting and oiling create barriers; galvanizing coats iron with zinc, which also protects sacrificially if scratched. Stainless steel contains chromium and often nickel. Alloys are mixtures whose different-sized atoms hinder layer slippage, increasing hardness or strength.

Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated, general formula CnH₂n+₂; alkenes contain a C=C bond, formula CnH₂n for open-chain compounds, and undergo addition reactions. Chemistry and Industry.intro: Chemical industries convert raw materials into useful products on large scales. Process design balances yield, rate, energy, safety, cost and environmental impact.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Haber and Contact processes; Feedstocks, reactors and separation; and Yield, atom economy and sustainability.

Important examples include Haber synthesis of ammonia, Contact-process manufacture of sulfuric acid, fractional distillation of crude oil, electrolysis of brine and extraction/refining of metals. Industrial decisions use equilibrium and rate principles: catalysts improve rate, higher pressure may improve gas yield but raises equipment cost, and temperature is chosen as a practical compromise. Atom economy = Mr of desired product/total Mr of products ×100%; percentage yield = actual yield/theoretical yield ×100%. Recycle unreacted feed where economical and control wastes and emissions.
Haber process: N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), exothermic; iron catalyst, elevated pressure, moderate temperature and recycling support efficient production.

The Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen; the Contact process makes sulfuric acid using sulfur dioxide oxidation to sulfur trioxide. Both use catalysts and equilibrium conditions chosen for a practical balance of yield, rate, energy and cost. A catalyst speeds approach to equilibrium but does not change equilibrium composition.

Industrial plants purify feed gases to prevent catalyst poisoning, control temperature and pressure, remove products and recycle unreacted feed. Removing a product can shift a reversible reaction toward more product. Heat exchangers may recover energy from hot streams. Continuous processing can improve throughput but demands reliable control and safety systems.

Percentage yield measures actual relative to theoretical product; atom economy measures how much reactant mass is incorporated into the desired product. A process with high yield can still generate large waste if atom economy is poor. Green chemistry seeks safer reagents, lower energy use, renewable feedstocks, catalysis and waste prevention.
